title: I want to end my life
a:
I'm really glad you told me. You matter, and you don't have to carry this alone.

Please reach out to someone right now:
• SADAG Suicide Crisis Line: 0800 567 567 (24 hours)
• Lifeline: 0861 322 322
• In immediate danger: 112

If you can, tell someone near you how you feel and stay with them. Put anything you could hurt yourself with out of reach. These feelings can change, and help works.

title: Self-harm urges
a:
Thank you for being honest. The urge to hurt yourself is a sign of deep pain, not a weakness, and you deserve care instead of more pain.

• Reach out now: SADAG 0800 21 22 23 or the Suicide Crisis Line 0800 567 567.
• Tell a person you trust how you feel, even just 'I'm struggling'.
• Move to a space where others are around, and keep sharp objects away.
• If you have hurt yourself badly, go to a clinic or call 112.

A counsellor can help you find safer ways to cope.

title: I was raped or sexually assaulted
a:
I'm so sorry. It is not your fault, and you deserve care and support.

1. Get to a safe place and, if you can, call someone you trust.
2. Go to a hospital, clinic or Thuthuzela Care Centre. HIV PEP works best within 72 hours, and emergency contraception works best as early as possible.
3. If you can, avoid washing or changing clothes before an exam, as this may preserve evidence. If you already have, you can still get care and report.
4. A doctor completes a medical report (the J88 form) if you decide to report.
5. GBV Command Centre (free, 24/7): 0800 428 428.

You choose if and when to report. Counselling is available whatever you decide.

title: I feel unsafe right now
a:
Your safety comes first.

• Head to a busy, well-lit place (shop, petrol station, security guard).
• Call 112 or 10111 now.
• Tap SOS in HerHub to alert your trusted circle with your location.
• If you are being followed, don't go home. Go to people.
• Make noise if needed: shout, or use the siren in HerHub.

title: My partner is abusive
a:
Thank you for trusting me. What's happening isn't your fault, and help is available.

• GBV Command Centre (free, 24/7): 0800 428 428
• Police: 10111, or 112 in an emergency
• You can apply for a protection order at the magistrate's court for free
• Strangulation is very dangerous even when there are no marks. Seek medical care.
• Build a safety plan in HerHub, and use Quick Exit if you need to hide the app

Would you like to know how to leave safely, or how a protection order works?

title: Signs of an abusive relationship
a:
Abuse is not only hitting. Common warning signs:
• Constant criticism, name-calling or humiliation
• Controlling who you see, where you go, your phone or your money
• Jealousy and accusations, checking your messages
• Threats, scaring you, breaking things
• Making you feel guilty or 'crazy' (gaslighting)
• Pressuring you into sex
• Cycles of cruelty followed by apologies and gifts

If several of these sound familiar, your feelings are valid. The GBV Command Centre (0800 428 428) can talk it through confidentially.

title: Coercive control
a:
Coercive control is a pattern of behaviour that takes away your freedom: controlling money, movement, clothes, friends, work, or monitoring your phone. It can happen without any physical violence and is still abuse.

What helps:
• Talk to someone outside the relationship
• Keep a private record of incidents (HerHub's private log)
• Make a safety plan before any big change
• Call 0800 428 428 for free counselling and options

title: Financial or economic abuse
a:
Financial abuse includes taking your salary or grants, hiding household money, forbidding you to work, running up debt in your name, or forcing you to sign documents.

• Open an account in your name only, if you can do so safely
• Keep copies of your ID, payslips and bank statements somewhere safe
• You may apply for maintenance for yourself and your children at the magistrate's court
• Legal Aid South Africa is free: 0800 110 110
• Check your credit report for debts you didn't take

title: How to get a protection order
a:
In South Africa you can apply for a protection order under the Domestic Violence Act, free of charge.

1. Go to the magistrate's court nearest you (or the police can help you).
2. Ask for the domestic violence clerk and complete the application. They must assist you.
3. A magistrate may grant an interim order straight away. It is served on the abuser, with a date to return to court.
4. On the return date the court decides on a final order.
5. Once he has been served, breaking the order is a crime. Keep a copy with you and note any breach.

You don't need a lawyer. Legal Aid: 0800 110 110. This is general information, not legal advice.

title: Protection from stalking or harassment
a:
The Protection from Harassment Act lets you apply for an order against someone who stalks or harasses you, including online, even if you were never in a relationship.

• Apply at the magistrate's court (harassment court clerk)
• Keep screenshots, call logs and dates as evidence
• Block, but save what they sent first
• You can also report to the police and ask for a case number

Legal Aid can help for free: 0800 110 110.

title: Leaving an abusive relationship safely
a:
Leaving is the most dangerous time, so plan if you can.

• Call the GBV Command Centre (0800 428 428). They can help find a shelter or safe house.
• Pack a hidden bag: ID, bank card, phone charger, medication, spare keys, some cash, children's documents.
• Choose a safe person who knows your plan and a code word to signal danger.
• Leave when the abuser is out, if possible, and don't tell him where you're going.
• Apply for a protection order and maintenance afterwards.
• If you are in danger now, call 112 or 10111.

Your private safety plan in HerHub can store your checklist.

title: Make a safety plan
a:
A safety plan is your personal checklist for staying safe. Include:
• Warning signs and safe rooms in the home (with exits, avoid kitchen or bathroom)
• A hidden emergency bag and spare keys
• Trusted people and a code word
• Important numbers: 112, 10111, 0800 428 428
• Copies of ID, protection order and medical records
• Where you would go and how you would get there

Open HerHub's Abuse & Harassment Support to build and keep yours privately.

title: Shelters and safe houses
a:
Shelters give women (and often children) a safe place to stay, plus counselling and practical help.

• Call the GBV Command Centre: 0800 428 428. They can refer you to a shelter near you.
• The Department of Social Development and local police stations also keep lists of shelters.
• Ask whether the shelter takes children and what to bring.
• Many shelters keep their address private for your safety.

If you are in danger tonight, call 112 or 10111.

title: Children affected by abuse
a:
Children are harmed by seeing violence too, and child abuse must always be taken seriously.

• Childline South Africa (free): 0800 055 555
• Police 10111, or 112 in an emergency
• Anyone who suspects abuse can report it to the police or a social worker
• Believe the child, stay calm, don't blame them, and get medical care if needed
• A protection order can name your children too

You are not overreacting by asking for help.

title: Helping a friend who is being abused
a:
You can make a big difference.
• Listen without judging. Say 'I believe you. It's not your fault.'
• Don't tell her to just leave. Leaving is complicated and risky.
• Offer practical help: a safe place to talk, a lift, storing documents
• Share the GBV Command Centre number: 0800 428 428
• Respect her choices, and keep checking in
• If she is in immediate danger, call 112 or 10111

Look after yourself too. Supporting someone is hard.

title: After a sexual assault: health steps
a:
Medical steps that protect your health:
• HIV PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis): start within 72 hours, the sooner the better
• Emergency contraception: as early as possible, up to 5 days depending on the type
• Testing and treatment for STIs, and a pregnancy test
• Care for injuries and emotional support

Thuthuzela Care Centres at many hospitals offer all of this in one place. If you can, don't wash before an exam, but you can still get care if you have.

GBV Command Centre: 0800 428 428 (free, 24/7).

title: Reporting a crime to the police
a:
You can report at any police station, and you have rights:
• Ask for a female officer and a private room
• Have a support person with you
• You must get a case number and a copy of your statement
• Police must help you get medical care and a protection order
• If police refuse or are rude, ask for the station commander, or complain to IPID or the Commission for Gender Equality
• You choose if and when to report. Sexual offence cases can be reported even years later

Crime Stop (anonymous tip-offs): 08600 10111.

title: Free legal help
a:
Free legal help in South Africa:
• Legal Aid South Africa: 0800 110 110
• Magistrate's court clerks can help with protection orders and maintenance applications
• Law clinics at universities
• Commission for Gender Equality and the Public Protector for complaints

HerHub's Know your rights guide in the Information Hub explains protection orders, harassment and reporting. This is general information, not legal advice.

title: Child maintenance
kw: he doesn't pay for the child
a:
Both parents must support their children, whether or not they were married.

• Apply at the maintenance court at your magistrate's court. It's free.
• Bring the child's birth certificate, your ID, proof of expenses and the other parent's details
• A maintenance officer helps you, and the court can order payments, even deducted from salary
• Not paying can lead to penalties
• Ask SASSA about child support grants too

Legal Aid: 0800 110 110.

title: Rape within a relationship
kw: no means no in a relationship
cant say no to my husband
a:
Sex without consent is rape, including in marriage or a relationship. In South Africa the law protects you.

• You can say no at any time, even if you said yes before
• Being pressured, threatened or too scared to say no is not consent
• You can report to the police, get medical care, and apply for a protection order
• GBV Command Centre: 0800 428 428

It is not your fault.

title: What is consent?
a:
Consent means a clear, free and enthusiastic yes, every time.
• It can be withdrawn at any moment
• Silence, being asleep, drunk or drugged, or scared is not consent
• Saying yes to one thing is not yes to everything
• Pressure, threats or manipulation cancel consent

If something happened that felt wrong, your feelings are valid and you can talk to a counsellor: GBV Command Centre 0800 428 428.

title: Sextortion and intimate image abuse
a:
Threatening to share intimate images is a crime. Under the Cybercrimes Act, sharing them without consent is also illegal.

• Don't pay. Payments usually lead to more demands.
• Stop replying, but save screenshots, usernames and links as evidence
• Report the account to the platform and ask them to remove the images
• Report to the police and ask for a case number
• You can apply for a protection order
• Tell someone you trust. This is not your fault.

Support: GBV Command Centre 0800 428 428.

title: Stalking
a:
Stalking is repeated, unwanted attention that makes you afraid. You can act on it:
• Keep a log with dates, times, screenshots and photos
• Tell trusted people, work and security
• Vary your routines and avoid sharing live locations
• Report to the police and request a case number
• Apply for a protection order under the Protection from Harassment Act
• Use HerHub's Trusted Circle and Safe Journey when going out

If you are in danger now, call 112 or 10111.

title: Phone or online monitoring
kw: check if my phone is monitored
a:
Signs your phone may be monitored: fast battery drain, unknown apps, unusual data use, or someone knowing things you never told them.

• Use a safe device (a friend's phone) to change passwords
• Review installed apps and permissions; remove anything you don't recognise
• Check 'linked devices' on WhatsApp and your social accounts
• Turn off location sharing, and check Find My Device or Google account access
• If it is serious, a factory reset can help. Back up first
• Keep evidence and report to the police

See HerHub's Digital & Personal Security checklist.

title: Workplace sexual harassment
a:
Sexual harassment at work is unlawful in South Africa, and your employer must act.
• Write down what happened: dates, times, witnesses
• Keep messages and emails
• Report in writing to your employer or HR and ask for the policy and process
• You can refer a dispute to the CCMA, or speak to a labour lawyer or Legal Aid (0800 110 110)
• You can also report to the police if it involves assault
• You may not be punished for reporting

You don't have to carry this alone.

title: Street harassment
a:
Street harassment is not your fault and you don't owe anyone a response.
• Move to a busy place and stay near other women or staff
• You can say a loud, firm 'Stop' to draw attention
• Note details: time, place, description, and report to the police or the transport operator
• If you are groped or exposed to, you can lay a charge
• Tell a friend and share your location

If you feel unsafe now, call 10111 or 112.

title: Human trafficking and fake job offers
a:
Warning signs: a job offer that is too good to be true, someone keeping your ID or passport, owing 'debt' you can't pay, being kept from leaving or contacting family.

• Human Trafficking Helpline (free): 0800 222 777
• Police: 10111, or 112
• Never travel for work unless you can verify the employer and keep your own documents
• Tell a trusted person your destination and share your location

You are not in trouble for being a victim.

title: Forced marriage or virginity testing
a:
No one may force you to marry, and a person under 18 cannot lawfully be married off. Forced marriage and ukuthwala are criminal.

• Call Childline (0800 055 555) if you are under 18
• Call the GBV Command Centre (0800 428 428) or the police (10111)
• The Commission for Gender Equality can also help
• You can get a protection order and be placed in a safe place

You have the right to say no.

title: Walking home safely
a:
For walking safely:
• Share your route and expected arrival time with someone. HerHub's Safe Journey does this with a check-in timer
• Stick to well-lit, busy streets, even if longer
• Keep your phone charged and one ear free of headphones
• Walk with purpose and look confident. Trust your gut if something feels off
• Have keys ready before you reach the door
• If you are being followed, cross the road, enter a shop, and call someone

Want me to open Safe Journey?

title: Taxi, minibus and ride-hailing safety
a:
For rides:
• Match the driver's name, plate and car to the app before getting in
• Share your trip with a trusted contact, and sit behind the front passenger seat if alone
• Keep your phone charged, and don't let the driver change the route without checking
• Wait inside a shop or building until the car arrives
• Avoid empty carriages and stay near the driver or other women on trains and buses
• If you feel unsafe, ask to be dropped at a busy place or call 112

Use Safe Journey to share your trip.

title: Driving, hijacking and car safety
a:
In a car:
• Lock doors and keep windows up in traffic; keep valuables out of sight
• Park in well-lit, busy places; check the back seat before you get in
• If someone tries to hijack you: stay calm, don't resist, hand over the vehicle, and get away safely. Your life matters more
• If a car flashes you or you are followed, drive to a police station or busy place
• For a breakdown at night, call someone and stay locked in. Hazards on
• If police stop you and you are unsure, drive slowly to a well-lit public place and ask for ID

Emergency: 112 or 10111.

title: Nights out, drink spiking
a:
Staying safe on a night out:
• Go with friends and agree to leave together. Check in with each other
• Watch your drink being poured, keep it in hand, and don't accept drinks from strangers
• Signs of spiking: sudden dizziness, confusion, blurred vision, nausea, memory gaps. Tell a friend or staff, and get to a safe place
• If you suspect spiking, go to a hospital as soon as you can. Tests are time-sensitive
• Have your own way home and charged phone
• Share your location with a trusted contact

If you were assaulted: 0800 428 428.

title: Online dating and meeting strangers
a:
Safer dating:
• Video call before meeting; reverse-search their photos
• Meet in a public place and arrange your own transport
• Tell a friend where you are and who you're with. Use Safe Journey
• Don't share your home address, workplace or financial details early on
• Watch your drink and keep your phone charged
• Red flags: refuses video calls, pushes quickly for love, asks for money or intimate photos
• Trust your gut. You can leave at any time

If someone asked for money, see my scam tips.

title: Home safety and living alone
a:
At home:
• Keep doors and windows locked, even when home. Good lighting outside
• Don't open the door to unknown people. Ask for ID through a window or intercom
• Don't announce on social media that you are alone or away
• Keep emergency numbers visible and a charged phone by the bed
• Know your neighbours, and join a community safety group
• If someone is inside, get out or lock yourself in a room, call 10111 or 112

HerHub's SOS can alert your Trusted Circle silently.

title: Safety during load-shedding
a:
During power cuts:
• Have torches, a charged power bank and your phone's flashlight ready
• Avoid walking in the dark. Plan trips around the schedule
• Keep gates and doors locked; traffic lights may be off, so drive carefully
• Let someone know where you are and when you expect to be home
• Check on neighbours who live alone

HerHub's siren and flashlight blink are available on the SOS screen.

title: Travelling safely
a:
Before you travel:
• Share your itinerary and accommodation with a trusted contact
• Keep copies of your ID and tickets, and save emergency numbers for where you're going
• Choose well-reviewed accommodation, and check locks on arrival
• Keep valuables hidden, avoid showing wealth, and don't hitchhike
• Set check-in times with a friend
• Outside South Africa, learn the local emergency number

HerHub's Safe Journey can be used for road trips too.

title: Self-defence and pepper spray
a:
Your best defence is avoiding danger, but these help:
• Use your voice: shout 'Back off!' or 'Fire!' to draw attention
• Target vulnerable areas (eyes, nose, throat, groin, knees) and then run to safety
• Pepper spray is legal to carry for personal protection in South Africa, but must be used responsibly. Keep it easy to reach and practise
• A personal alarm or HerHub's siren draws attention
• A short self-defence class builds confidence

You are never to blame for not fighting back. Survival comes first.

title: Using the siren and flashlight
a:
HerHub's panic siren is a real, loud emergency siren at full volume. The flashlight blinks 10 times when it starts to draw attention.

• Open Personal Safety & Emergency and tap 'Sound siren', or use the Panic siren shortcut on Home
• Tap again to stop
• Turn on 'Also sound the siren' under Hands-free SOS to play it automatically
• Make sure silent or do-not-disturb mode isn't muting alarms on your phone

Want me to open it?

title: Campus and school safety
a:
On campus:
• Save campus security's number and share your route when walking after dark
• Use well-lit paths and walk with friends
• Report harassment or assault to campus protection services, the university's gender-based violence office, and the police
• Universities must have policies against sexual misconduct. Ask for them
• Look after friends at parties and agree to leave together

Support: GBV Command Centre 0800 428 428.

title: ATM and money safety
a:
At the ATM:
• Use machines inside banks or well-lit, busy places
• Cover the keypad when entering your PIN. Never accept 'help' from strangers
• If the card is stuck or swallowed, call your bank from the number on the card, don't leave it
• Don't count cash in public, and stay aware of who is behind you
• Use your banking app instead when possible

Never share your PIN or OTP with anyone.

title: GBV and abuse helplines
kw: who do i call for abuse
a:
Free help for gender-based violence in South Africa:
• GBV Command Centre (24/7, free): 0800 428 428
• Stop Gender Violence Helpline: 0800 150 150
• TEARS Foundation USSD: *134*7355# (free 'Please call me')
• Childline: 0800 055 555
• Human Trafficking Helpline: 0800 222 777
• Police: 10111, Emergency: 112

Tap a number to call. You can see more in the Emergency Resource Directory.

title: Mental health helplines
a:
Support lines in South Africa:
• SADAG: 0800 21 22 23
• SADAG Suicide Crisis Line: 0800 567 567
• SADAG 24-hour helpline: 0800 12 13 14
• Lifeline: 0861 322 322
• Emergency: 112

You can also visit a public clinic for referral to a counsellor. You deserve support.

title: Emergency numbers
a:
Key emergency numbers (South Africa):
• 112 from any mobile phone
• Police: 10111
• Public ambulance: 10177
• Crime Stop: 08600 10111
• GBV Command Centre: 0800 428 428

In an emergency, HerHub's SOS screen has call buttons and can alert your Trusted Circle.

title: Late or missed period
a:
Periods can be late because of stress, illness, travel, weight change, intense exercise, hormones (like PCOS or thyroid), breastfeeding, perimenopause, or pregnancy.

• If you've had unprotected sex, take a pregnancy test (most work from the first day of a missed period)
• See a clinic if you miss three periods in a row, are not pregnant, or also have unusual symptoms
• Track your cycle in HerHub to see patterns

This is general information, not a diagnosis.

title: Period pain and cramps
a:
Period pain is common. What can help:
• A hot water bottle or warm bath
• Gentle movement or stretching, and rest
• Water, and regular meals
• Over-the-counter pain relief such as ibuprofen or paracetamol, if it's safe for you. Follow the label

See a healthcare professional if pain is severe, is getting worse, stops you from daily life, or doesn't respond to pain relief. It could be endometriosis or another condition.

title: Heavy periods
a:
Seek care if you:
• Soak a pad or tampon every hour for several hours
• Pass clots bigger than a coin
• Bleed for more than 7 days
• Feel dizzy, faint or very tired (possible anaemia)

Causes include fibroids, hormonal imbalance, polyps, and other conditions. Treatments are available. Ask your clinic. If you are pregnant or could be, heavy bleeding is urgent: go to a clinic or hospital.

title: PMS and PMDD
a:
PMS includes mood changes, bloating, tender breasts, tiredness and cravings in the week or two before a period.

• Regular sleep and exercise help
• Eat balanced meals, and cut back on caffeine and salt
• Log symptoms in HerHub to see your pattern

If mood symptoms are severe (intense sadness, anger, hopelessness), it could be PMDD. Talk to a healthcare professional. Treatment can help. If you feel hopeless, call SADAG 0800 21 22 23.

title: Spotting between periods
a:
Light spotting can happen with ovulation, new contraception, stress or hormonal changes. See a clinic if it keeps happening, occurs after sex, after menopause, or comes with pain or heavy bleeding.

If you could be pregnant and have bleeding with one-sided pain, go to a clinic or hospital urgently (ectopic pregnancy can be dangerous).

title: PCOS
a:
PCOS (polycystic ovary syndrome) is a common hormone condition. Signs include irregular or missing periods, acne, extra facial or body hair, scalp hair thinning, and weight gain. It can affect fertility.

• A clinic can check hormones and do an ultrasound
• Healthy eating, movement and sleep help many people
• Medication can regulate periods or help with symptoms or pregnancy

It's manageable. Ask your clinic or doctor.

title: Endometriosis
a:
Endometriosis is when tissue similar to the womb lining grows elsewhere, causing severe period pain, pelvic pain, pain during sex, heavy bleeding, and sometimes fertility problems. It's often missed for years.

If pain disrupts your life, see a doctor or gynaecologist. Keep a symptom diary in HerHub to show them. Treatments include pain relief, hormonal treatment and sometimes surgery.

title: Fibroids and cysts
a:
Fibroids are non-cancerous growths in the womb, and ovarian cysts are fluid-filled sacs. Many cause no symptoms, but some cause heavy periods, pelvic pressure, pain, frequent urination or bloating.

See a clinic or doctor for a check and ultrasound. Sudden severe pelvic pain, fainting or fever needs urgent care.

title: Vaginal discharge, thrush and BV
a:
Some discharge is normal and changes with your cycle. See a clinic if you notice:
• Strong or fishy smell
• Green, yellow or grey discharge
• Itching, burning or soreness
• Pain, or sores

Thrush (thick, white, itchy) and BV (fishy smell) are common and treatable. STIs can cause similar symptoms, so it's best to get tested. Avoid douching or scented products, wear breathable cotton, and don't self-treat repeatedly.

title: Urinary tract infections
a:
Signs of a UTI: burning when you pee, needing to go often, cloudy or strong-smelling urine, lower tummy pain.

• See a clinic. Antibiotics are usually needed
• Drink plenty of water, and wipe front to back
• Pee after sex

Go urgently if you have fever, back or side pain, vomiting, or blood in the urine (kidney infection), or if you're pregnant.

title: STIs and testing
a:
Many STIs have no symptoms, so testing is the only way to know. Symptoms may include unusual discharge, pain when peeing, sores, itching, lower tummy pain or pain during sex.

• Public clinics offer free STI and HIV testing and treatment
• Most STIs are curable; others can be managed
• Tell your partner(s) so they can be treated too
• Condoms reduce risk

A nurse will treat you without judgement.

title: HIV, PrEP and PEP
a:
• Testing is free and confidential at public clinics
• PEP: pills taken within 72 hours after possible exposure (e.g., assault or condom failure) to prevent HIV
• PrEP: daily medicine that greatly lowers HIV risk, available at many clinics
• Treatment (ART) allows people with HIV to live long, healthy lives. When the viral load is undetectable the virus can't be passed on sexually (U=U)
• In pregnancy, treatment protects the baby

National AIDS Helpline: 0800 012 322 (free).

title: Contraception and birth control
a:
Common options at public clinics (free):
• Condoms: protect against pregnancy and most STIs
• Pill: daily; works if taken on time
• Injection: every 2 or 3 months
• Implant: lasts about 3 years
• IUD (copper or hormonal): lasts several years
• Permanent options: tubal ligation (for those sure they're done)

A nurse can help you choose. Contraception doesn't protect you from STIs unless you also use a condom. You're allowed to choose, and nobody can force a method on you.

title: Emergency contraception
a:
Emergency contraception can prevent pregnancy after unprotected sex or contraceptive failure.
• Morning-after pills work best as early as possible, within 72 hours (some work up to 5 days)
• A copper IUD fitted by a clinic within 5 days is the most effective option
• Available free at public clinics and at pharmacies
• It does not end an existing pregnancy

If you are worried about HIV, ask about PEP as well (within 72 hours). Take a pregnancy test if your period is late.

title: Cervical screening, HPV and smears
a:
Cervical cancer is largely preventable.
• Public clinics offer free Pap smears from age 30 (ask your clinic about the schedule, and sooner if you live with HIV)
• The HPV vaccine is offered to girls in public schools, and protects against the virus that causes most cervical cancers
• Condoms reduce risk, but don't remove it
• Report bleeding after sex, between periods or after menopause

Regular screening finds problems early, when they're easiest to treat. CANSA: 0800 22 66 22.

title: Breast health
a:
Get to know how your breasts normally look and feel. See a clinic if you notice:
• A new lump or thickened area
• Dimpling, redness or skin changes
• Nipple turning inward, or discharge (especially bloody)
• Persistent one-sided pain

Most lumps aren't cancer, but must be checked. Ask your clinic about mammograms, usually from around 40 or earlier if there's family history. CANSA: 0800 22 66 22.

title: Perimenopause and menopause
a:
Perimenopause (often from the 40s) brings irregular periods, hot flushes, night sweats, sleep problems, mood changes and vaginal dryness. Menopause is confirmed after 12 months without a period, on average around 51.

• Regular exercise, sleep and less alcohol or caffeine can help
• Treatments (including HRT) are available. Talk to a doctor
• Keep up bone health and screening
• Seek help for heavy bleeding or bleeding after menopause

title: Iron and anaemia
a:
Heavy periods, pregnancy and low-iron diets can cause anaemia: tiredness, pale skin, dizziness, shortness of breath, headaches.

• Eat iron-rich foods (red meat, liver, beans, lentils, dark leafy greens), with vitamin C (citrus, peppers)
• Limit tea or coffee with meals, which lowers iron absorption
• Clinics can test and provide iron tablets
• Don't self-medicate with high iron doses without advice

title: Period products and hygiene
a:
• Change pads or tampons every 4 to 8 hours. Never leave a tampon in for more than 8 hours
• Menstrual cups can stay in up to 12 hours; sterilise between cycles
• Use the lowest absorbency you need
• Wash hands before and after, and avoid scented products
• Toxic shock syndrome is rare but serious: sudden fever, rash, dizziness or vomiting while using a tampon means remove it and go to hospital
• If you can't afford products, clinics, schools, NGOs and community programmes may help

title: How the period tracker works
a:
Log the first day of each period in HerHub, and I'll estimate your next period, ovulation and fertile window. More cycles make predictions more accurate.

• Tap 'My period started today' or choose a date
• Add flow, symptoms and notes in the daily log
• Predictions are estimates, not medical advice or contraception

Want me to open the Period tracker?

title: Am I pregnant? Testing
kw: how do i know if im pregnant
a:
Early signs: missed period, nausea, tender breasts, tiredness, needing to pee often. Most home tests work from the first day of a missed period. Test in the morning and repeat after a few days if negative and your period hasn't come.

• Clinics test for free and can confirm
• If positive: go for antenatal care early; avoid alcohol and smoking; ask about folic acid
• If you are unsure what to do, a counsellor can talk through all your options (see 'termination')

If you have bleeding with one-sided pain, seek urgent care.

title: Pregnancy care and antenatal visits
a:
If you're pregnant:
• Visit a clinic as early as you can for antenatal care and an HIV test. Keep every appointment
• Folic acid is usually recommended before and early in pregnancy. Ask your clinic
• Avoid alcohol and smoking, and ask a professional before taking any medicine
• Eat varied, nourishing food, drink water, rest, and move gently
• Use HerHub's Pregnancy tool for your due date and weekly progress

Go urgently for bleeding, severe pain, severe headache, blurred vision, or if your baby moves much less.

title: Morning sickness and nausea
a:
Nausea is common in early pregnancy and often eases after the first trimester.
• Eat small, frequent snacks; keep crackers by the bed
• Sip fluids, try ginger or cold foods, avoid triggers
• Rest and fresh air help

See a clinic if you can't keep fluids down, are losing weight, are very dizzy, or have dark urine. That may be hyperemesis, which needs treatment.

title: Pregnancy danger signs
kw: when to go to hospital pregnant
a:
Go to a clinic or hospital urgently, or call 112, if you have:
• Vaginal bleeding
• Severe abdominal pain
• Severe headache, blurred vision, sudden swelling of face or hands (possible pre-eclampsia)
• Baby moving much less than usual
• Fluid leaking or waters breaking, or regular contractions before 37 weeks
• Fever or feeling very unwell

Don't wait for a scheduled visit.

title: Miscarriage and pregnancy loss
a:
I'm so sorry. Pregnancy loss is painful, and grief is normal. It's not your fault.

• Heavy bleeding, fever, severe pain or fainting: go to a hospital urgently
• A clinic can confirm what's happening and help with care
• Give yourself time to grieve; you may want to talk to someone. SADAG: 0800 21 22 23
• Most people who miscarry go on to have healthy pregnancies, when they feel ready

title: Ectopic pregnancy
a:
An ectopic pregnancy (outside the womb) is an emergency. Warning signs: one-sided lower abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, dizziness or fainting, pain at the tip of the shoulder.

Go to a hospital immediately or call 112.

title: Termination of pregnancy
kw: pregnant and dont want the baby
a:
In South Africa, the Choice on Termination of Pregnancy Act gives you the right to choose.
• On request up to 12 weeks, at designated public facilities, free of charge
• From 13 to 20 weeks under certain conditions (for example risk to health)
• Nobody can force you. If you're under 18, you're encouraged (not required) to involve an adult
• Pre- and post-abortion counselling is available
• Don't use unregulated 'backstreet' providers or unsafe pills. They can be dangerous

Go to a clinic as early as possible. Ask for a referral. You will be treated without judgement.

title: Labour and birth
a:
Signs of labour: regular, strengthening contractions that get closer together, a 'show' of mucus or blood, or waters breaking.

• Go to the clinic or hospital when contractions are about 5 minutes apart for an hour, your waters break, you have bleeding, or baby moves less
• Pack your bag early: Road to Health card, ID, clothes for you and baby
• You can ask questions and have a birth companion
• Arrange transport in advance

If in doubt, call your clinic or 112.

title: Breastfeeding
a:
Breastfeeding is recommended exclusively for the first 6 months, if you can. Tips:
• Feed on demand and make sure baby latches deeply
• Sore nipples often improve with a better latch. Ask the nurse or lactation consultant
• Red, hot, painful breast with fever may be mastitis. See a clinic
• Living with HIV? Follow your treatment, as clinics give guidance on safe feeding
• Fed is best. If you can't breastfeed, you haven't failed

Ask your clinic about support groups.

title: Newborn care
a:
Basics for newborns:
• Keep your Road to Health booklet and attend immunisation visits
• Keep baby warm, clean the cord stump dry, and always place baby to sleep on the back
• Feed often, and watch wet nappies
• Go to a clinic urgently if baby has a fever, is floppy or very sleepy, struggles to breathe, won't feed, or has yellow skin that spreads
• Crying can be hard. If you feel overwhelmed, put baby down safely and take a breath. Never shake a baby

Childline: 0800 055 555.

title: Postnatal depression
a:
Many mothers feel tearful in the first two weeks (baby blues). If sadness, anxiety, numbness, guilt or thoughts of harming yourself or your baby last longer, it may be postnatal depression. It's common and treatable, and it isn't your fault.

• Tell your clinic nurse or doctor
• SADAG: 0800 21 22 23. Lifeline: 0861 322 322
• Rest when you can, accept help, and talk to someone
• If you have thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, call 0800 567 567 or 112 now

title: Trying to conceive
a:
To improve your chances:
• Have sex every 1 to 2 days in your fertile window (the days before and on ovulation). HerHub estimates it from your cycle
• Take folic acid, eat well, avoid smoking and alcohol, and keep a healthy weight
• Most couples conceive within a year. If you're under 35 and haven't after 12 months (or 6 months if over 35), see a doctor
• Irregular cycles, PCOS and STIs can affect fertility. Both partners can be tested

Open the Pregnancy & Fertility tool to see your window.

title: Healthy eating
a:
Simple, nourishing habits:
• Fill half your plate with vegetables and fruit, add protein and whole grains
• Include iron (beans, greens, meat), calcium (milk, yoghurt, leafy greens) and healthy fats
• Drink water through the day. HerHub can remind you
• Limit sugary drinks and ultra-processed foods
• Don't skip meals or follow extreme diets

If you're worried about eating or body image, you can talk to a counsellor.

title: Hydration
a:
Most adults do well with around 6 to 8 glasses of fluid a day, more in heat, exercise, pregnancy or breastfeeding. Pale yellow urine is a good sign.

Log your glasses in HerHub's Health & Wellness page, and turn on the Drink water reminder in Smart Notifications.

title: Exercise and movement
a:
Aim for movement most days. Even a 20 to 30 minute walk helps your heart, mood and sleep.
• Pick something you enjoy
• Gentle exercise can ease period pain
• Warm up, stay hydrated, and rest when needed
• Walk or run in safe, well-lit places, or with a friend. Share your route using Safe Journey
• Check with a doctor if you're pregnant, recovering or have a medical condition

title: Sleep and insomnia
a:
For better sleep:
• Keep a regular bedtime and wake time
• No screens for 30 minutes before bed, and keep the room cool and dark
• Limit caffeine after midday, and heavy meals late
• Try slow breathing or a body scan. HerHub has guided breathing
• Write worries in a journal before bed

If poor sleep lasts weeks, or you have nightmares after trauma, see a healthcare professional.

title: Headaches and migraines
a:
Many headaches ease with water, rest, a dark quiet room, and regular meals. Hormone changes can trigger migraines around periods.

See a doctor urgently for a sudden severe headache, headache with fever and stiff neck, vision changes, weakness, confusion, or a headache in pregnancy with swelling or blurred vision (possible pre-eclampsia).

title: Basic first aid
a:
For emergencies call 112 or 10177. Basics until help arrives:
• Bleeding: press firmly with a clean cloth
• Burns: cool under running water for 20 minutes
• Choking: encourage coughing; if it fails, give back blows then abdominal thrusts
• Fainting: lay the person down and raise legs
• Poisoning: call the Poisons Helpline 0861 555 777

A first-aid course is a great skill to learn.

title: Anxiety and panic
a:
That sounds really hard. Try this now:
• Breathe in for 4, hold 4, out for 4, hold 4. Repeat a few rounds
• Ground yourself: name 5 things you see, 4 you feel, 3 you hear, 2 you smell, 1 you taste
• Remind yourself: 'This will pass. I am safe right now.'

I can open guided breathing in HerHub. If anxiety keeps happening for weeks, talk to a clinic or SADAG (0800 21 22 23). Panic attacks are frightening but not dangerous.

title: Grounding and calming exercises
a:
A few quick ways to calm your body:
• Box breathing: in 4, hold 4, out 4, hold 4
• 5-4-3-2-1 senses grounding
• Press your feet into the floor, and notice the support beneath you
• Splash cool water on your face
• Name what you feel: 'I feel scared, and I'm safe right now'

HerHub's Mental Health page has a guided breathing circle.

title: Sadness and depression
a:
I'm sorry you're feeling this way. Your feelings are valid, and depression is a health condition, not a weakness.

• Reach out to someone you trust today, even with a short message
• Try one small kind thing: a shower, a walk, a meal
• Keep a mood log in HerHub to spot patterns
• If this has lasted more than two weeks, or you feel hopeless, please talk to a clinic or counsellor. SADAG: 0800 21 22 23
• If you think about ending your life: 0800 567 567 or 112

title: Loneliness and isolation
a:
Feeling lonely is human, and many people feel it. Small steps help:
• Message one person today
• Join a group around something you enjoy: sport, church, study, volunteering
• Spend time outside, around other people
• HerHub's Support & Community can connect you with others

If the loneliness feels heavy or hopeless, talk to someone: SADAG 0800 21 22 23 or Lifeline 0861 322 322.

title: Trauma and PTSD
kw: cant stop thinking about what happened
a:
After something frightening or violent, it's common to have flashbacks, nightmares, being jumpy, numbness, or avoiding reminders. These are normal reactions to abnormal events. They often ease with time, but support helps.

• You didn't cause it, and you're not weak
• Talk to a trauma counsellor, doctor or support group
• Grounding and breathing can help in the moment
• GBV Command Centre: 0800 428 428. SADAG: 0800 21 22 23

If symptoms last more than a month or you feel unsafe, get professional help.

title: Finding counselling or therapy
a:
Options in South Africa:
• SADAG: 0800 21 22 23 (referrals to affordable help)
• Public clinics and community health centres: ask for a mental health nurse or referral
• Lifeline: 0861 322 322 (counselling)
• Universities and employers often provide counselling
• Private psychologists. Some medical aids cover sessions

You don't need to be in crisis to ask for support.

title: Burnout and stress
a:
Burnout shows up as exhaustion, cynicism and feeling ineffective. What helps:
• Rest, boundaries and saying no to extra tasks
• Break big jobs into small steps
• Move your body and spend time with people who lift you
• Talk to a manager, lecturer or counsellor about your load
• Short breathing breaks during the day

If it lasts or affects your health, see a professional.

title: Grief and loss
a:
I'm so sorry for your loss. Grief has no timetable, and it can bring sadness, anger, numbness and waves of emotion.
• Let yourself feel, and talk about the person
• Keep to simple routines: food, water, sleep
• Lean on family, friends or your community. Faith or support groups can help
• Reach out for counselling if grief feels stuck or unbearable: SADAG 0800 21 22 23

title: Self-esteem and body image
a:
You are worthy as you are. Some ideas:
• Notice self-criticism and respond as you would to a friend
• Limit social media that makes you feel less than
• List three things your body did for you today
• Move and eat for health and joy, not punishment
• Talk to someone you trust or a counsellor

HerHub's daily affirmations are in the Mental Health page.

title: Eating disorders
a:
If food, weight or your body is taking over your thoughts, you deserve support. Eating disorders are real and treatable, and they can affect anyone.

• Speak to a doctor, clinic or counsellor. SADAG can refer you: 0800 21 22 23
• Tell someone you trust
• Try not to weigh yourself or avoid food as punishment
• Seek urgent help if you feel faint, have chest pain, or think about harming yourself

Recovery is possible.

title: Anger and relationships
a:
Strong feelings are part of relationships. Helpful steps:
• Pause, breathe, and step away before reacting
• Use 'I feel...' statements and listen to the other person
• Healthy relationships have respect, trust and safety. Fear, control or violence is not normal
• After a breakup, give yourself time to grieve. Talk to friends or a counsellor

If you feel afraid of your partner, see the abuse information, or call 0800 428 428.

title: Alcohol and drugs
a:
If alcohol or drugs are affecting your life, help is available without judgement.
• SADAG substance abuse line: 0800 12 13 14
• Clinics can refer you for treatment, and many areas have support groups
• If someone you love drinks and becomes violent, your safety comes first. See GBV help, 0800 428 428
• Never drink and drive, and watch your drink when out

Small steps count.

title: Spotting scams
a:
Scam red flags: urgency or threats, requests for your OTP, PIN or password, links to unfamiliar sites, strange sender numbers, prizes you didn't enter for, and offers that are too good to be true.

• Banks will never ask for your PIN, password or OTP
• Don't click links. Type the website yourself
• Call your bank on the number on your card
• Paste the suspicious message here and I'll check it for you
• Report to your bank, and to the FSCA: 0800 20 3722

title: OTP and PIN safety
a:
Never share your OTP, PIN, password, CVV or verification code, not even with someone who says they are from your bank, the police or a delivery company. They are the keys to your money and accounts.

If you shared one by mistake, call your bank immediately on the number on your card, block the card, and change your passwords.

title: SIM swap and account takeover
a:
A SIM swap is when criminals move your number to a new SIM to receive your OTPs. Warning signs: your phone suddenly loses network for no reason, and you get messages about SIM or account changes.

• Call your mobile provider and bank immediately from another phone
• Ask them to block your SIM and review recent transactions
• Change passwords and turn on two-factor authentication using an authenticator app
• Report to the police and keep a case number

title: I've been scammed: what to do
a:
Act quickly:
1. Call your bank on the number on your card, and ask them to block your cards and stop transactions
2. Change passwords for banking, email and social media
3. Contact your mobile provider if a SIM swap is suspected
4. Report to the police and get a case number
5. Report to the FSCA (0800 20 3722). You may also lodge a complaint with the Ombudsman for Banking Services (0860 800 900)
6. Keep evidence: screenshots, messages and receipts

It's not your fault. Scammers are professionals.

title: Romance and investment scams
a:
Common patterns: someone you've never met builds a quick, deep bond, then has an emergency needing money; or promises huge, guaranteed returns.
• Never send money, gift cards or crypto to someone you haven't met in person
• Check financial providers are registered with the FSCA
• If it sounds too good to be true, it is
• Talk to someone you trust before sending money

If you've lost money: see 'I've been scammed'. FSCA: 0800 20 3722.

title: Loan sharks and debt
a:
If you're in debt:
• Use registered credit providers (check with the National Credit Regulator). Unregistered lenders (mashonisas) often charge illegal interest and may hold your card or ID. That's illegal
• Never give away your bank card or PIN
• A debt counsellor can help you restructure repayments
• Know your rights: debt collectors may not threaten or harass you
• Legal Aid: 0800 110 110

Ask for help before things spiral.

title: Budgeting and saving
a:
A simple plan:
• List your income and must-pay costs first (housing, food, transport)
• Try 50/30/20: needs, wants, savings. Adjust to your situation
• Start a small emergency fund, even R50 a week. It builds safety
• Use a stokvel or savings account with no easy withdrawals
• Track spending for a month

HerHub's Financial Safety page has a savings goal tracker. Want me to open it?

title: Passwords and account security
a:
Protect your accounts:
• Use long, unique passwords (a password manager helps) and don't reuse them
• Turn on two-factor authentication, using an app where possible
• Review privacy settings, and who can see your location and photos
• Log out of old devices and check 'linked devices'
• Lock your phone with a PIN or biometric, and hide notification previews
• If someone controlling or abusive knows your passwords, change them from a safe device

See HerHub's Digital & Personal Security.

title: How does SOS work?
kw: how do i send an alert
how do i get help in the app
a:
Tap SOS on Home to open Personal Safety & Emergency. From there you can:
• Call 112, Police 10111 or Ambulance 10177
• Alert your Trusted Circle with an SMS and map link
• Sound the loud siren, with 10 flashlight blinks
• Follow the 'If you feel unsafe' steps

HerHub doesn't dispatch emergency services itself. Always call them directly in danger.

title: Hands-free SOS (power button)
a:
Hands-free SOS lets you trigger help without opening the app: press the power button twice quickly, even with the screen off. You get a 5-second chance to cancel, then HerHub texts your Trusted Circle your location, and can sound the siren and call your first contact.

Turn it on in Personal Safety & Emergency. Set HerHub to 'Unrestricted' battery use so Android keeps it running, and test it. Don't rely on it alone.

title: Trusted Circle
a:
Your Trusted Circle is the people who receive your alerts. Add at least one person: name, phone number and relationship. When you tap 'Alert my trusted circle', or when SOS fires, HerHub sends them an SMS with your location link.

• Choose people who will answer and can reach you
• Tell them they're on your circle, so they know what to do
• Keep numbers up to date

Want me to open Trusted Circle?

title: Safe Journey
a:
Safe Journey is a trip timer with a safety check-in:
1. Enter your destination and how many minutes you expect to take
2. HerHub reminds you to check in when time is up
3. Tap 'I've arrived safely', or alert your circle if something is wrong
4. You can add 15 minutes if you're delayed

Use it for walks home, rides, dates and trips. Want me to open it?

title: Safety Map
a:
The Safety Map shows your location and community safety notices. You can:
• Tap Me to centre on your position
• Report an incident to warn others
• Tap Help to find nearby police, hospitals and clinics

Maps are © OpenStreetMap contributors. Reports are community information, not verified by emergency services.

title: Your privacy in HerHub
a:
• Without an account, your data stays on this phone
• With an account, your data backs up to your private account space
• Your period, mood and journal entries are never shown to others
• Use Quick Exit in Abuse & Harassment Support to close the app fast
• You can clear data or delete your account in Digital & Personal Security
• Hide notification previews on your lock screen if someone else may see your phone

HerHub is a support tool, not emergency services.

title: Reminders and notifications
a: In Smart Notifications you can switch on daily reminders for water, medication, mood check-ins, safety check-ins and logging your period, and pick the time for each. If reminders don't appear, allow notifications for HerHub in your phone's settings.

title: Dark mode and appearance
a: Go to More > Appearance and choose Light, Dark or Auto (follows your phone). All HerHub screens and icons adapt automatically.

title: What can you do?
a:
I'm your HerHub guide. I run privately on your phone and don't send your chats anywhere.

Ask me about:
• Safety: walking home, rides, dates, drink spiking, stalking
• Abuse and GBV: protection orders, leaving safely, helplines
• Health: periods, pregnancy, contraception, STIs, menopause
• Mind: anxiety, sadness, trauma, sleep
• Money: scams, OTPs, budgets, debt
• HerHub features: SOS, siren, Trusted Circle, Safe Journey

I'm not a doctor, lawyer or emergency service. In danger, call 112 or 10111.

title: Say hello
a: Hi, I'm your HerHub guide. I can give general safety, health and wellbeing guidance, and open the right tool for you. What's on your mind?

title: Thank you
a: You're welcome. I'm glad I could help. You're not alone, and I'm here whenever you need me.

title: Goodbye
a: Take care of yourself. Remember: your safety comes first, and help is always one tap away in HerHub.

title: How are you?
a: I'm here and ready to help. How are you feeling today? You can tell me, or tap one of the topics below.

title: Something light
a:
Here's a little smile: Why did the scarecrow win an award? Because he was outstanding in his field.

If you're really struggling and not just needing a laugh, I'm here for that too.

title: Encouragement
a: You are allowed to take up space. Your feelings are valid, and they will change. Asking for help is strength, and one small step is still progress. You deserve safety, rest and kindness, today and every day.
